newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE decides to send observers to Chechnya polls.
newsitem.headline: OSCE decides to send observers to Chechnya polls.

text.p: Europe's top security body said on Thursday it would send observers to post-war elections in Chechnya but could not guarantee their safety.

"We are planning to send observers to the election. It has been agreed," said Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen of Denmark, which took over the chairmanship of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) this month.
"But I would give no guarantees that we might not have mishaps, it would not be reasonable to do," he told a news conference after addressing the OSCE permanent council.

Petersen said the OSCE had provided around $300,000 to fund the elections, due to be held on January 27. He rejected criticism by Russian politicians that the action was a breach of Russian law, which bars foreign funding of local elections.

"I think the Russian objections are built on misunderstandings of what the OSCE does in these situations...This is not a financing of election campaigns, this is financing an election," Petersen said.

"My message is that we are not interfering in the political process of Chechnya or Russia but we are contributing to the holding of elections," he added. "That is the backbone of the OSCE's activity."
But in Moscow, the liberal head of parliament's foreign affairs committee described the behaviour of Swiss diplomat Tim Guldimann, who heads the OSCE mission in Chechnya, as "very strange".
Vladimir Lukin praised parliament and his committee for starting an investigation into the money, which he said the diplomat had given to the Chechen authorities.
He told a news conference that if it turned out Guldimann had not had permission to deliver the money, he should go.

"If one of the other federal bodies agreed to it they should say so...If he did this without agreement at his own risk or for some reason by order of someone else, I say if, he must be withdrawn immediately without any discussion," Lukin said.
Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Guldimann as saying the issue had been agreed with Moscow: "All the OSCE mission's actions are agreed with the federal (Russian) side."

The OSCE's participation in the supervision of the polls was thrown into question after a spate of recent violence in Chechnya, including the shooting of a group of Russians and the murder of six foreign Red Cross workers.
But Petersen said it was important for foreign observers to be present at the elections. Between 60 and 70 monitors are expected to supervise the polls.

"We feel confident that it is responsible to send this observer mission, also from a security point of view," he said. "If, in the time before the elections, incidents occur that change this picture we will at very short notice be able to call off the observer mission."
The elections are backed by the Russian authorities, despite unresolved differences over the issue of the republic's independence after 21 months of bitter conflict.

Under a deal struck in August Moscow and the rebels agreed to postpone the issue of Chechnya's political status for five years in return for a withdrawal of Russian troops from the region. Russia announced on January 5 it had pulled out its last Interior Ministry troops from the province.
The separatists are keen to have observers at the voting to add legitimacy to the elections, which they see as a first step towards international recognition of Chechen independence.
Petersen said the mechanics of the voting, particularly for the mainly Russian refugees living outside Chechnya, was still under discussion by the Russians and Chechens.
